question: What are the de-facto standard semantics for CriticMarkup-in-Markdown, as established by existing open-source implementations across all parser architectures and languages? Catalog every findable OSS Markdown+CriticMarkup implementation, extract the concrete language-definition decisions each made from primary sources (source code, test suites, docs, issue-tracker rulings), and identify where consensus exists versus where implementations diverge — so that a new editor engine (MarkText's document-core) can adopt established practice instead of inventing semantics. The findings will feed a normative md+cm specification and the design of an O(n), incrementally-reparsing, error-tolerant editor parser. Background: CriticMarkup defines {++addition++}, {--deletion--}, {~~old~>new~~}, {==highlight==}, {>>comment<<} in a short prose spec that does not define interaction with Markdown structure; every implementation had to decide the open questions itself. Implementations to examine (all languages/architectures; plus any others found): MultiMarkdown (C, by CM co-creator Fletcher Penney); the original CriticMarkup toolkit (Python, Sublime/BBEdit); CodeMirror lang-criticmarkup and other CM CodeMirror extensions (overlay vs nested parse); Obsidian Commentator and other CM plugins; Pandoc CriticMarkup filters (Lua/Python) and any official Pandoc position; markdown-it / remark-unified / Python-Markdown CM plugins; Zettlr, Ghostwriter, other OSS editors; Vim/Emacs CM modes; any Rust/Go/Swift CM packages; and (as secondary documented-behavior evidence only) iA Writer, Marked 2, Ulysses. For EACH implementation, extract its answer to these 11 questions, citing the file/test/doc that proves it, saying undefined/untested where never decided: (1) Multi-block spans — can an annotation cross a blank line or block boundary (paragraph-spanning deletion, annotation spanning a blockquote or list)? Or confined to a single block? If block-level changes are supported, what syntax is required (markers on their own lines)? (2) Literal precedence — is {++ inside inline code, fenced code, math, autolink, or raw HTML a marker or literal text, and is that decided in one pass or by processing order? (3) Markdown inside annotations — is Markdown parsed inside annotation arms? Inside comments and highlights too? (4) Delimiter containment — can emphasis/link state opened inside an arm match a closer outside it? Same across the ~> separator of a substitution. (5) Nesting — can CM annotations nest, and what actually happens on nested input? (6) Accept/reject semantics — what exactly do accept-all and reject-all produce; when accepting/rejecting changes block structure (deletion spanning a heading marker, addition containing a blank line), is the result re-parsed; do tools operate on source text or a parsed tree? (7) Highlight-comment pairing — is {==...==}{>>...<<} an attached pair; is a standalone comment anchored to anything? (8) Escaping — any way to write a literal {++ outside code? (9) Structural interactions — GFM tables (pipes inside annotations), lists (annotations spanning items), front matter, footnotes. (10) Unclosed markers — behavior on an opening marker with no closer (a permanent state during live typing); error tolerance and mid-edit rendering. (11) Parse architecture — regex prepass vs integrated single-pass grammar vs overlay/mixed parsing vs post-processing, and known ordering bugs of each. Deliverables: a per-implementation decision matrix (11 questions x implementations with citations); a consensus analysis per question (de-facto standard answer by majority or by the authoritative implementations MultiMarkdown + original toolkit, versus irreconcilable divergence); any formal specification efforts beyond the prose spec (proposed grammars, EBNF, CommonMark forum track-changes threads, spec repos) and their status; and a recommended best-existing-practice profile — for each of the 11 questions the answer a new implementation should adopt for ecosystem compatibility, explicitly flagging where consensus implies accepting a limitation (e.g. single-block confinement of annotations) and where no consensus exists so a new implementation must decide itself. Prefer primary sources; report test-suite evidence wherever it exists.
summary: Across the three implementations with verified primary-source evidence — MultiMarkdown-6 (C, by CriticMarkup co-creator Fletcher Penney), the original CriticMarkup toolkit (Python), and lang-criticmarkup (Lezer/CodeMirror 6) — the de-facto standard treats CriticMarkup as a lexically simple, Markdown-blind layer: annotation contents are opaque text at parse time, delimiters that straddle Markdown inline spans are explicitly unsupported, there is no escaping mechanism, and no implementation exempts code spans or fences from marker recognition. The clearest architectural consensus is Penney's own ruling that CriticMarkup is an orthogonal layer ideally processed as a separate pass over source text: the original toolkit is a pure regex prepass before Markdown conversion, MMD-6's accept/reject is an Aho-Corasick source-text prepass that erases byte ranges before Markdown parsing, and lang-criticmarkup mounts a standalone plain-text grammar as an overlay via parseMixed. The sharpest divergence is multi-block spans (Q1): MMD-6's rendering path confines annotations to a single block while the reference toolkit's DOTALL regexes deliberately match across blank lines (with ad-hoc   surgery for paragraph breaks), and Penney floated but never implemented a markers-on-own-lines block syntax. Accept/reject semantics are firmly settled by MMD-6's test suite (accept keeps additions/drops deletions, reject inverts; highlights keep content and comments are erased under both), unclosed markers degrade gracefully to literal text, and {==...==}{>>...<<} adjacency is a recommended convention codified as a combined regex in the toolkit but parsed as two sibling nodes in lang-criticmarkup.

findings.claim:
Q1 (multi-block spans) is the sharpest divergence: MultiMarkdown-6's rendering path confines CriticMarkup to a single block — annotations spanning a paragraph or list-item boundary are not recognized and degrade to literal text — while the original CriticMarkup toolkit's reference parsers deliberately permit multi-paragraph spans via (?s)/re.DOTALL regexes, handling crossed blank lines with ad-hoc string surgery (deletion of exactly "

" renders <del> </del>; additions touching "

" get <ins class='critic break'> </ins> placeholders; interior newlines flattened to spaces), even as the prose spec warns authors to avoid newlines in tags. lang-criticmarkup's grammar imposes no line/block restriction at all (block behavior is delegated to the host Markdown parse).
findings.evidence: MMD-6 docs: "CriticMarkup must be contained within a single block (e.g. paragraph, list item, etc.) CM that spans multiple blocks will not be recognized"; Penney in issue #41: "For now, CriticMarkup doesn't play well 'across' paragraphs in MMD." Toolkit: all five patterns carry (?s), e.g. r'''(?s)\{\+\+(?P<value>.*?)\+\+...\}''', with dedicated \n\n branches in additionProcess/deletionProcess. lang-criticmarkup: Addition { AdditionStart Content* AdditionEnd } with no newline-sensitive token.

findings.claim: Q1 block-level syntax: the markers-on-their-own-lines convention for block-level CriticMarkup was proposed by Penney himself in MMD-6 issue #41 ("Require that such CriticMarkup start and end with the opening/closing tags on their own separate lines... treat it as its own block") but was never implemented; the issue remains open, so no implementation among those verified ships a defined block-level-change syntax.
findings.evidence: Penney: "This could allow the MMD parser to recognize a CriticMarkup 'chunk' and treat it as its own block"; concluded "I will consider ways of addressing this in the future" — verifier confirmed no later implementation.

findings.claim: Q11 (parse architecture): the authoritative design position and dominant practice is CriticMarkup as a Markdown-blind pass over source text. Penney's primary-source ruling: CriticMarkup "is orthogonal to... Markdown/MultiMarkdown. It should really be thought of as a separate 'layer' of markup — one that needs to be processed _before_ parsing the underlying MultiMarkdown." The original toolkit implements exactly this: five sequential whole-document re.sub passes (order: deletions, additions, comments, highlight+comment, substitutions) emitting <ins>/<del>/<mark> HTML, then piping to markdown/markdown2/multimarkdown — cross-type interactions are decided purely by pass ordering. MMD-6's accept/reject is likewise a source-text prepass (Aho-Corasick trie tokenizer over the raw buffer, token-pair matching, byte-range erasure via d_string_erase, run in main.c before Markdown conversion). lang-criticmarkup takes the overlay variant: a standalone Lezer grammar mounted atop the Markdown parse via parseMixed, not an extension of the Markdown grammar. Important caveat: MMD-6's rendering path is NOT a prepass — a claim that MMD-6 resolves CM before all other processing was refuted 0-3; rendering integrates CM tokens into the per-block inline token-pair engine, which is precisely why it inherits single-block confinement.
findings.evidence: Toolkit spec: "Markup syntax should be easily parsed with simple regular expressions"; critic.py's five re.sub calls then subprocess.Popen(['/usr/local/bin/multimarkdown']). MMD-6: trie_insert(ac, "{++", CM_ADD_OPEN)... ac_trie_leftmost_longest_search; main.c runs mmd_critic_markup_accept(buffer) before conversion when EXT_CRITIC_ACCEPT set. lang-criticmarkup README: parseMixed with overlay "Parse everything and mount the result as overlays".
findings.vote: claims 4, 6, 11, 14, 16, 20 (all 3-0); refuted claim on MMD-6 universal prepass (0-3) noted; merged

findings.claim: Q2 (literal precedence) and Q8 (escaping): no verified implementation protects code contexts or provides an escape. The original toolkit's parsers apply CM regexes to raw text before Markdown conversion with zero exemption for inline code, fenced code, or HTML — a {++...++} inside code is consumed as a marker — and no backslash or other escape mechanism exists anywhere in the code. MMD-6's accept/reject Aho-Corasick tokenizer is equally Markdown-blind (no backtick/fence/block checks in critic_markup.c). Markers win everywhere; literal {++ outside code is unwritable in these tools.
findings.evidence: Verifiers inspected both toolkit processors line-by-line: no code-context detection, no escape handling; code handling delegated to downstream Markdown extensions ('fenced-code-blocks', 'codehilite') after CM substitution has already happened. MMD-6 critic_markup.c contains no checks for backticks, fences, blank lines, or HTML.

findings.claim: Q3 (Markdown inside annotations) and Q4 (delimiter containment): consensus is that annotation arms are opaque at CM-parse time and Markdown delimiters must be fully contained within an arm. The toolkit README mandates "Wrap Markdown Tags Completely... the CriticMarkup processor currently chokes on them", requiring {~~*italic fonts*~>*italic font-styles*~~} with complete emphasis pairs per substitution arm. MMD-6 documents the same limitation: "CriticMarkup that crosses multiple MultiMarkdown (MMD) spans (e.g. {++** foo} bar**) will not properly manage the intended MultiMarkdown markup." lang-criticmarkup's grammar treats all annotation bodies as catch-all Content* tokens with no Markdown productions (Markdown inside arms, if rendered, comes only from the separate host parse). No implementation supports emphasis/link state straddling an annotation boundary or the ~> separator.
findings.evidence: Verbatim README guidance and MMD-6 limitations section confirmed by verifiers; lang-criticmarkup grammar: @local tokens with @else Content, bodies defined solely as Content*.

findings.claim: Q5 (nesting): divergent. MMD-6 deliberately supports nested annotations in accept/reject — all five pair types registered with PAIRING_ALLOW_EMPTY | PAIRING_PRUNE_MATCH, children processed recursively, and CuTest proves it: accepting {++foo{--bat--}bar++} yields "foobar"; rejecting {--foo{-- bat --}bar--} yields "foo bat bar". lang-criticmarkup's grammar does not admit nesting (bodies are Content*, not the statement alternation), so an inner opener falls to Lezer's generic error recovery with no defined semantics and no nested test cases. The toolkit's non-greedy flat regexes give ordering-dependent, undesigned behavior.
findings.evidence: MMD-6: token_pair_engine_add_pairing(...PAIRING_ALLOW_EMPTY | PAIRING_PRUNE_MATCH); accept_token recurses via accept_token_tree on children; three nesting tests verified in-source. lang-criticmarkup: verifier confirmed no annotation rule references 'statement' and no nested test fixtures exist.

findings.claim: Q6 (accept/reject semantics) is firmly settled by MMD-6, the only verified implementation with executable accept/reject: --accept yields the 'new' document (addition content kept sans delimiters, deletions erased entirely, substitution keeps new arm), --reject yields the 'original' (inverse); highlights keep their inner text with delimiters stripped under BOTH modes; comments are erased entirely under BOTH modes. Operations are performed on raw source text (DString byte-range erasure), not a parsed tree, and the edited source is subsequently re-parsed as ordinary Markdown — so block-structure changes are resolved by the downstream Markdown parse, and since the accept/reject scanner runs over the whole buffer ignoring blank lines, multi-block annotations DO work in accept/reject mode even though rendering rejects them. Proven by embedded CuTest assertions ({++foo bar++} accept→"foo bar"/reject→""; {--foo bar--} accept→""/reject→"foo bar"; {==foo bar==}→"foo bar" both; {>>foo bar<<}→"" both).
findings.evidence: Doc: "CriticMarkup comments and highlighting are ignored when processing with --accept or --reject." Source: accept_token/reject_token erasure matrix and CuTest suite verified verbatim; mmd_critic_markup_accept(DString *d) operates on the raw buffer before mmd conversion.

findings.claim: Q7 (highlight-comment pairing): the pairing is a recommended convention, not a structural requirement. The toolkit spec says a highlight "can be used on its own" but recommends it "always be followed by a comment", and its parsers codify adjacency with a dedicated combined regex {\=\=...\=\=\}\{\>\>...\<\<\} applied before the standalone-comment regex. lang-criticmarkup parses {==...==}{>>...<<} as two independent sibling nodes with no pair construct (proven by its test fixture). MMD-6's accept/reject gives comments no special treatment when preceded by a highlight — comments are always dropped ({++foo++}{>>bar<<} accept→"foo"). Standalone comments are anchored to nothing in any verified implementation.
findings.evidence: Toolkit mark_pattern = r'''(?s)\{\=\=(?P<value>.*?)\=\=\}\{\>\>(?P<comment>.*?)\<\<\}'''; lang-criticmarkup expected tree: CriticMarkup(Content, Highlight(...), Comment(...), Content) as siblings; MMD-6 combined test verified.

findings.claim: Q10 (unclosed markers): the best-articulated behavior is MMD-6's graceful degradation — in accept/reject, any open/close marker token with no matched mate (t->mate == NULL) is skipped and left in the output as literal text; only mated pairs are erased, and nothing is consumed to end-of-document (empirically compiled and confirmed by a verifier: "{++ok++} and {++unclosed" accept→"ok and {++unclosed"). Rendering-path unmatched markers likewise fall through to literal output (html.c prints "{++"). Exception found by the verifier: a stray ~> divider (CM_SUB_DIV) is unconditionally erased, so the substitution divider is not error-tolerant. lang-criticmarkup handles unclosed markers via Lezer's generic error recovery producing error nodes (its test suite includes start-missing and end-missing cases); the toolkit's regexes simply fail to match an unclosed opener, leaving it literal.
findings.evidence: Verified switch: case CM_ADD_OPEN... if (!t->mate) { break; } before d_string_erase; verifier compiled the C sources and confirmed byte-identical passthrough of unclosed markers under both accept and reject, plus the CM_SUB_DIV counterexample.

findings.claim: Q9 (structural interactions — tables, lists, front matter, footnotes) and much of Q3-for-comments are undefined/untested in every verified implementation: no test suite or doc among MMD-6, the toolkit, or lang-criticmarkup addresses pipes-in-annotations in GFM tables, annotations spanning list items (beyond MMD-6's blanket single-block rule making them unrecognized), front matter, or footnotes. The surviving evidence base covers only these three implementations; the many others in the research brief (Pandoc filters, markdown-it/remark plugins, Obsidian Commentator, Zettlr's editor integration, iA Writer/Marked 2 documented behavior, formal spec efforts) produced no claims that survived adversarial verification.
findings.evidence: Absence-of-evidence finding: verified test suites (MMD-6 CuTest, lang-criticmarkup lezer fixtures covering additions/deletions/substitutions/highlight-comment only) contain no structural-interaction cases; this is an inference from the surviving claim set rather than a positively verified assertion.

findings.claim: Recommended best-existing-practice profile for a new editor engine (MarkText document-core): treat CM as a distinct lexical layer with opaque arms (Q3/Q4 — require fully-contained Markdown per arm, matching toolkit guidance and MMD-6's documented limitation); confine annotations to a single block in the rendering parse (Q1 — MMD-6's rule, the authoritative WYSIWYG-relevant precedent) while implementing accept/reject as source-text edits followed by re-parse (Q6 — MMD-6's tested model, which incidentally tolerates multi-block spans at accept time); support nesting per MMD-6's tested recursive semantics (Q5); let code/math contexts win over CM markers (Q2) — here a new implementation must knowingly DIVERGE from the reference tools, which have no literal precedence, because an integrated editor parser cannot ship code-blind CM; provide no escape mechanism beyond code spans (Q8 — none exists in the ecosystem); treat {==}{>>}<< adjacency as a loose sibling pairing recognized by adjacency, not a grammar construct (Q7); leave unclosed markers as literal/error-recovered text without consuming to EOF (Q10 — MMD-6 + Lezer precedent); and use overlay/two-layer parsing (lang-criticmarkup's parseMixed pattern) or integrated inline tokens rather than a destructive regex prepass (Q11), since the prepass architecture is where all known ordering bugs live (toolkit pass-ordering dependence, code-context blindness).
sources: synthesis of all confirmed claims above
findings.evidence: Each element traces to a confirmed finding; the Q2 divergence recommendation is a normative judgment (all verified implementations lack literal precedence, but that behavior is universally regarded as a defect — Penney's own docs list these as 'limitations'), not an observed consensus.

caveats: Coverage is narrow: only three implementations (MultiMarkdown-6, the original CriticMarkup toolkit, and nathanlesage/lang-criticmarkup) produced claims that survived verification, so the 'de-facto standard' here rests on the two authoritative implementations plus one modern CM6 grammar — the brief's other targets (Pandoc filters, markdown-it/remark/Python-Markdown plugins, Obsidian Commentator, Zettlr's shipped integration, Vim/Emacs modes, Rust/Go/Swift packages, iA Writer/Marked 2/Ulysses documented behavior, and any formal spec/EBNF efforts) are unevidenced in this synthesis and the consensus analysis could shift if they were examined. One claim was refuted (0-3): MMD-6 does NOT resolve CriticMarkup as a prepass for rendering — only for accept/reject — so statements about 'MMD-6's architecture' must distinguish the two code paths; Penney's prepass position (issue #41, 2017) is design philosophy, not shipped rendering behavior. The MMD-6 single-block claim [0] passed only 2-1, though it was independently corroborated 3-0 by claim [3] and the official docs. The toolkit repo has been dormant since ~2013 and its DOTALL multi-block behavior contradicts its own prose guidance, so 'reference behavior' and 'reference recommendation' diverge within the same project. Time-sensitivity is low (all three codebases are stable/frozen), but lang-criticmarkup is a small single-author package and weaker precedent than the other two. The Q9 structural-interactions finding and the best-practice profile are inferences/normative synthesis, not directly verified claims.
openQuestions: What semantics do the unexamined mainstream plugin ecosystems (Pandoc CriticMarkup filters, markdown-it/remark/Python-Markdown extensions, Obsidian Commentator's CM6 state-field approach) implement for the 11 questions — in particular whether any of them DOES give code spans literal precedence over CM markers, which would establish precedent for the recommended Q2 divergence?

Do any formal specification efforts beyond the prose spec exist (CommonMark forum track-changes threads, proposed EBNF/grammars, spec repos), and did any reach a ruling on block-level annotation syntax such as Penney's markers-on-own-lines proposal from MMD-6 issue #41?

How do MMD-6's rendering path and accept/reject path interact on the same document containing multi-block annotations (rendered as literal text but silently transformed by --accept) — is this render/accept asymmetry a known bug-report topic, and should a new implementation reproduce or reject it?

What is the actual runtime behavior (not just grammar-level undefinedness) of lang-criticmarkup/Lezer error recovery and of Zettlr's production editor on nested and unclosed annotations during live typing — the mid-edit tolerance scenario most relevant to an incrementally-reparsing editor parser?

refuted.claim: MultiMarkdown-6's parse architecture handles CriticMarkup as a prepass: CriticMarkup is resolved before any other MultiMarkdown (Markdown) processing occurs, rather than being integrated into the Markdown grammar.
